title: the Rajasuya
hook: Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna walk into Jarasandha's city dressed as snatakas, refuse his welcome, and name themselves at midnight
carry: they gave their names, and their reason

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rajasuya almost given up, then Jarasandha's birth: two halves — the one joined by Jara. Did you answer someone's caution? Day seven hundred fifty-four.

Three men walk into the capital of Magadha wearing the dress of snatakas, young brahmanas who've just finished their studies. They have garlands on, and sandal paste. They don't come in by the main gate, which is a strange way for students to arrive anywhere. And they walk straight into the king's presence. Jarasandha stands up to receive them as honored guests. He has no idea that Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna are standing in his hall.
screen: `DRESSED AS SNATAKAS.` → `NOT BY THE MAIN GATE.` → `THE KING STANDS TO GREET THEM.`

segments.voice: Jarasandha does everything a good host should. He offers water, honors, a seat. And they won't take it. Krishna speaks for the group. My two companions, he says, are keeping a vow of silence until midnight. Then they'll speak. So the king leaves, and comes back at midnight, and now he asks the questions he's been holding. Snatakas don't usually wear garlands and paste like this. Your arms are marked like the arms of men who draw bows. You came in by a wrong way. And you refused my worship. Who are you? Krishna's answer is careful, and it's honest. A snataka, he says, enters a friend's house by its gate, and an enemy's house by another way. And we don't accept worship from an enemy. Jarasandha is puzzled. I've never wronged you, he says. Then Krishna names the wrong. You've captured kings and mean to offer them up as a sacrifice. We've come to free them. And he tells the king exactly who they are. Notice how strange this is. The disguise gets them through the door. But once they're inside, they don't hide why they came. They refuse the welcome. Some readers say that accepting it would have made them guests, and a guest can't rightly fight his host. They wait until he asks. Then they tell him their names and their reason. Jarasandha answers just as plainly. I took those kings in war, he says, and I won't let them go out of fear. Fight me, one of you, or two, or all three. He looks the three of them over, and he chooses Bhima.
screen: `THEY REFUSE THE WELCOME.` · `MIDNIGHT: WHO ARE YOU?` · `A FOE'S HOUSE, ANOTHER WAY IN.` · `NAMES AND REASONS, PLAINLY.` · then, large: `HE CHOOSES BHIMA.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind a hard conversation you've had, or one that's coming. Notice what you're carrying into it. Is anything disguised? Is there a welcome you'd be accepting that you don't mean to keep? Picture saying your reason plainly, the way Krishna does at midnight. You don't need to say it to anyone yet. Just let it be clear to you. The bell holds the time.
The Rajasuya. Today it runs through Jarasandha's hall at midnight, where three guests refuse his welcome and tell him why they've come.
Your line: they gave their names, and their reason. Today, if you disagree with someone, say your reason plainly, once, without dressing it up. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: A snataka is a student who has completed Vedic study and taken the ritual bath that ends it; Hindu tradition sets out a snataka's conduct, which is why Jarasandha notices that his guests don't look the part.

original.note: Sanskrit snātaka: a student who has completed study and taken the bath that ends it; the dress Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna wear.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sneak attack in disguise.
what it means: a disguise that gets them in, then plain names and reasons once they're asked.
what a scholar hears: Krishna says a snataka takes no worship from a foe; some readers add that this keeps them from becoming guests who fight their host.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Jarasandha-vadha Parva (the journey to Girivraja in snataka dress; the vow of silence until midnight; Krishna's answer; Jarasandha chooses Bhima)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm: snataka dress, garlands and sandal paste; entry not by the main gate; Jarasandha receiving them with honors.
Confirm Krishna's statement that his companions keep silence until midnight, and Jarasandha's midnight questions, including the bowstring marks on their arms.
Confirm Krishna's reply that a snataka enters a friend's house by the gate and a foe's by another way, and won't accept worship from a foe.
Confirm Jarasandha's reply: took the kings in war, won't release them from fear, offers to fight one, two or all three, and chooses Bhima.
The trapdoor's third floor (refusing worship keeps them from being guests) is an interpretation; a Keeper may wish to soften it.

Audit: the teach said "nobody lies about anything" once inside, which overstates (the disguise and the midnight delay are themselves concealment); now "they don't hide why they came". Trapdoor third floor now attributes the guest reading to some readers and keeps the text's own reason.
Details such as breaking drums on Chaityaka hill were left out as uncertain.
Editor pass: cut the unsourced 'they carry no visible weapons'; the teach's claim that guests can't fight their host is now framed as some readers' view, not the narrator's.
